choices.text: The electrons fly off faster, because the brighter beam hits harder
The electrons fly off more slowly, because they share the extra light
Brightness means more photons, not stronger ones: a dim violet beam ejects faster electrons than a bright red one.
Emission stops, because the plate is overwhelmed by light

questions.explanation: The trap claim is: Brighter light ejects faster electrons. Brightness feels like strength, so more light looks like harder hits. Brightness means more photons, not stronger ones: a dim violet beam ejects faster electrons than a bright red one. At the same frequency each photon still carries the same energy h f, so the brighter beam ejects more electrons, each with the same maximum kinetic energy as before.
questions.prompt: Ultraviolet light shines on a metal plate and electrons are emitted. The lamp is made much brighter at exactly the same frequency. A student claims the electrons now fly off faster. What actually happens?

choices.text: 0 J, because a single photon carries no energy

questions.explanation: Photon energy is E = h f: 6.63 x 10^-34 x 7.5 x 10^14 = 4.97 x 10^-19 J. Frequency alone sets the size of the packet - brightness only changes how many such packets arrive each second.
questions.prompt: What is the energy of one photon of light of frequency 7.5 x 10^14 Hz? (h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s)

questions.explanation: Einstein’s equation h f = W + KE_max balances the books: the photon energy first pays the work function, and the remainder is the electron’s maximum kinetic energy, 4.65 x 10^-19 J.
questions.prompt: Ultraviolet light of frequency 1.20 x 10^15 Hz strikes a metal of work function 3.31 x 10^-19 J. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons, showing your working with Einstein’s photoelectric equation.

questions.answer: λ = h / (m v) = 6.63 x 10^-34 / (9.11 x 10^-31 x 1.0 x 10^6) = 7.3 x 10^-10 m. A moving electron carries a wavelength just like a photon: matter shows wave-particle duality.
questions.explanation: de Broglie’s relation λ = h / (m v) gives every moving particle a wavelength; for this electron it is 7.3 x 10^-10 m, atomic in scale, which is why electron diffraction is observable.
questions.prompt: An emitted electron moves at 1.0 x 10^6 m s^-1. Calculate its de Broglie wavelength and say what this wave behaviour of matter is evidence for. (m_e = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg, h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s)

choices.text: The electrons need more time to soak up the light gradually
Each red photon carries less than the work function, and one electron absorbs only one photon, so no electron can pay the exit energy
The red light is reflected before it can do anything
The metal is already full of electrons at the surface

questions.explanation: Emission is a one-photon, one-electron exchange: below the threshold frequency each photon carries h f < W, so however many arrive, and however long they arrive for, no single electron ever receives enough energy to escape - exactly the silence in scene s2.
questions.prompt: Red light below the threshold frequency of a metal shines on it for a long time at high intensity, and no electrons are emitted. Why not?
